title: The Gita Beside Other Scriptures
bigQuestion: What can we learn by reading the Gita beside other scriptures on duty, nonviolence and devotion, without ranking any of them?

story.title: Letters Between Two Farms
story.kicker: A letter from Gandhi reaches Tolstoy, but a book of Tolstoy's reached Gandhi first.
paragraphs: In 1894, a young Indian lawyer in South Africa read a book that he later said overwhelmed him. It was The Kingdom of God Is Within You by the Russian novelist Leo Tolstoy, a Christian who had come to believe that the Sermon on the Mount forbids all violence. The lawyer was Mohandas Gandhi.

In 1908 Tolstoy wrote "A Letter to a Hindu," a reply to an Indian nationalist. In it he argued that Indians should resist British rule not with violence but by refusing to cooperate with evil, and he quoted the Hindu scriptures as well as the Gospels. Gandhi read the letter and wrote to Tolstoy in 1909, asking to publish it. Tolstoy agreed.

They wrote to each other until Tolstoy's death in 1910. Gandhi named a community farm near Johannesburg "Tolstoy Farm." There, people of different religions lived and worked together. Gandhi read the Gita every day; he also read the Sermon on the Mount, the Quran and the Buddha's teachings.

Later, in the United States, a young Baptist minister named Martin Luther King Jr. studied Gandhi. In 1959 he traveled to India to learn more. King drew on the Sermon on the Mount, as Tolstoy had, and on Gandhi's nonviolent method, which Gandhi linked to the Gita.

This chain of readers crosses religions and continents. In this chapter you will read the Gita beside other scriptures on three themes: duty and conscience, nonviolence, and devotion. The goal is to understand each text better, not to decide which is best.
story.think: Gandhi, Tolstoy and King each read another religion's scripture closely. What might a reader gain from that, and what might they miss?

lessons.title: Comparison Without Ranking
lessons.mainIdea: Comparing scriptures means placing them side by side to see each more clearly, not deciding which one is true or better.
reading: Comparative religion is an academic field that studies religions side by side. A good comparison places two texts next to each other on a shared question, such as "What should I do when duty and feeling clash?" It then notes how each text answers, in its own terms. Scholars call the shared question the *tertium comparationis*, the third thing that makes comparison possible.

A good comparison notices differences as carefully as likenesses. It is tempting to say that all scriptures teach "the same thing." Many scholars warn that this can erase what makes each tradition itself. The Gita's karma yoga and the Dhammapada's teaching on action are related, but they rest on different views of the self.

A good comparison also avoids *ranking*. In a public school, we do not declare one scripture truer, wiser or more advanced than another. We describe each fairly, attribute each belief to its tradition, and let the comparison show what each text cares about. Students may hold their own views, but essays in this course argue about meaning, not about truth.

words.d: the academic study of religions side by side
the shared question or feature that makes two things comparable
ordering things from better to worse; avoided in academic comparison of religions

look.title: Two Kinds of Comparison
look.text: Comparison A: "The Gita and the Sermon on the Mount both teach love, so they are really the same." Comparison B: "Both speak of acting without seeking reward, but the Gita grounds this in the self's freedom from results, while Matthew grounds it in the Father who sees in secret."
look.prompt: Which comparison teaches you more about each text? What does Comparison A lose?

check.q: What is the tertium comparationis?
choices: The shared question that makes two things comparable
check.why: It is the common ground of a comparison.

check.q: Why do many scholars warn against saying all scriptures teach the same thing?
choices: It is too hard to say
It can erase what makes each tradition itself
check.why: Real differences matter for understanding each text.

check.q: What does this course avoid when comparing scriptures?
choices: Ranking them as truer or better
check.why: Academic comparison describes without ranking.

lessons.title: Reading Across Traditions
lessons.mainIdea: Each scripture has its own language, setting and community, so a fair comparison names them for every text.
reading: The texts in this chapter come from very different worlds. The Gita is Sanskrit poetry inside a Hindu epic. The Book of Job is Hebrew poetry in the Jewish and Christian Bibles. The Dhammapada is a Pali collection of the Buddha's sayings. The Analects are Chinese sayings of Confucius. The Sermon on the Mount is Greek, in the Gospel of Matthew.

Each text also has a living community that reads it. Jews read Job in the Hebrew Bible, Christians in the Old Testament. Theravada Buddhists chant the Dhammapada. Confucian tradition shaped schools and families across East Asia. A fair comparison names the community each time, so that a reader never mistakes one tradition's belief for another's.

Translations matter too. When we quote the Gita we name Telang or Arnold. When we paraphrase other scriptures, we still say which text and passage we mean: Job 38, Dhammapada 5, Analects 15.24, Matthew 5:44. *Citation* lets any reader check our work, and it shows respect for each tradition's own words.

words.d: a Pali collection of the Buddha's sayings in 423 verses
the collected sayings of Confucius, compiled by his followers
Jesus's teaching in Matthew 5–7
naming the exact text and passage one is quoting or paraphrasing

look.title: Five Scriptures at a Glance
rows: Sermon on the Mount: chapters of Matthew
look.prompt: These texts differ greatly in form. How might a short saying collection and a long poem teach differently?

check.q: In what language is the Dhammapada preserved in the Theravada tradition?
check.why: The Theravada Dhammapada is in Pali.

check.q: Where is the Sermon on the Mount found?
check.why: The Sermon on the Mount is in Matthew's Gospel.

check.q: Why should a comparison name each text's community?
choices: Because all communities are the same
So no one mistakes one tradition's belief for another's
check.why: Naming communities keeps attribution accurate.

lessons.title: Arjuna and Job
lessons.mainIdea: Arjuna and Job both face terrible situations and question, and both receive a vast vision of the divine in reply, as their texts tell it.
reading: In the Book of Job, a righteous man loses his children, his wealth and his health. His friends insist he must have sinned. Job refuses to accept this and demands an answer from God. In chapters 38 to 41, God answers out of a whirlwind, asking Job where he was when the foundations of the earth were laid, and showing the vastness of creation.

Readers of the Gita often notice a likeness. Arjuna, too, faces an unbearable situation and questions what is right. He, too, receives a vision of the divine, the universal form in Gita 11, which overwhelms him. Both men respond with awe. Both texts treat human understanding as small beside what they present as the divine view.

The differences are just as important. Job suffers and protests injustice; Arjuna hesitates to act. In Jewish and Christian readings, God speaks as Creator, distinct from creation. In many Hindu readings, the universal form shows all beings existing within Krishna. The two scenes answer different questions in different ways, and each community reads its own text in its own light.

words.d: a book of the Hebrew Bible about a righteous man's suffering and God's answer
an attempt to explain why suffering exists if God is good
the storm from which God speaks to Job in Job 38

look.title: Two Visions
look.text: Job 38 (paraphrase): God asks Job, from the whirlwind, where he was when the earth's foundations were laid. Gita 11 (paraphrase): Arjuna sees all the worlds within Krishna's form, with the light of a thousand suns.
look.prompt: What does each vision answer, and what does it leave unanswered? How is each hero changed by what he sees?

check.q: From where does God answer Job?
check.why: Job 38 begins with God speaking from the whirlwind.

check.q: What is one difference between Job and Arjuna?
choices: Job is a warrior; Arjuna is a farmer
Job protests suffering; Arjuna hesitates to act
Job receives no answer; Arjuna receives none
check.why: Their situations and questions differ.

check.q: What is theodicy?
choices: An attempt to explain suffering if God is good
check.why: The Book of Job is often discussed as theodicy.

lessons.title: Action and Its Fruits in the Dhammapada
lessons.mainIdea: The Dhammapada, like the Gita, teaches that the mind shapes action, but it grounds this in the Buddha's teaching of no fixed self.
reading: The Dhammapada opens with a famous pair of verses. The mind comes first, it says; all things are made by mind. If one speaks or acts with a corrupted mind, suffering follows as the wheel follows the ox. If one speaks or acts with a pure mind, happiness follows like a shadow that never leaves.

The Gita also teaches that the state of mind behind an action matters, as in its teaching of action without attachment. Both texts use the word *karma* for action and its results. Both urge self-control. Many readers find in both a practical ethics of watching one's own mind.

But Buddhists and Hindus understand the self very differently. The Gita teaches an eternal self, atman, that is not slain. The Buddha, as Buddhists understand his teaching, taught anatman, "no fixed self." So even where the ethics sound alike, the reasons behind them differ. A careful comparison names that difference rather than hiding it.

words.d: action and its results; used in Hindu, Buddhist and Jain texts in related but different ways
"no fixed self"; the Buddhist teaching that there is no permanent, unchanging self
the study of right and wrong action

look.title: Mind and Action
look.text: Dhammapada 1–2 (paraphrase): mind comes first; act with a corrupt mind and suffering follows like the wheel behind the ox; act with a pure mind and happiness follows like a shadow. Gita 2.48 (paraphrase): act steady in yoga, the same in success and failure.
look.prompt: What do both passages say about the mind behind an action? What different view of the self stands behind each?

check.q: What does Dhammapada 1 say follows an action done with a corrupted mind?
choices: Suffering, as the wheel follows the ox
check.why: The famous image is the wheel following the ox.

check.q: What is anatman?
choices: The Buddhist teaching of no fixed self
The eternal self of the Gita
check.why: Anatman contrasts with the Gita's atman.

check.q: Why do the Gita and Dhammapada differ even where their ethics sound alike?
choices: They rest on different views of the self
They were written by the same person
check.why: Atman and anatman ground their ethics differently.

lessons.title: Role and Rightness in the Analects
lessons.mainIdea: The Analects and the Gita both link right action to one's role, but Confucius stresses learning, ritual and relationships.
reading: The Analects of Confucius, compiled by his students in China after his death in 479 BCE, teach how to become a *junzi*, an exemplary person. In Analects 12.11, Confucius says good order comes when the ruler is a ruler, the minister a minister, the father a father and the son a son. Each person should fulfill the role they hold.

The Gita's teaching of svadharma, one's own duty, in 3.35 also links right action to one's role. Readers often compare the two. Both texts value doing one's part well within a larger order. Both treat family and social duties seriously. Each also warns against people who ignore their duties to others.

Yet the grounds differ. Confucius rarely speaks of gods or the afterlife and says he transmits the ways of the ancients. He stresses learning, ritual propriety (li) and humaneness (ren). The Gita grounds duty in Krishna's teaching about the self and God. In Analects 15.24 Confucius gives a principle close to the Golden Rule: do not impose on others what you do not wish for yourself.

words.d: the exemplary or noble person in the Analects
humaneness or goodness toward others; a central virtue in the Analects
ritual propriety; right conduct in ceremonies and relationships

look.title: Analects 15.24
look.text: Asked if there is one word to live by, Confucius answers: reciprocity. Do not impose on others what you do not wish for yourself.
look.cite: Analects 15.24, paraphrased from James Legge, The Chinese Classics, vol. 1 (1861)
look.prompt: How does this principle compare with the Gita's teaching on svadharma? Is it about roles, or about all people equally?

check.q: What is a junzi?
choices: The exemplary person in the Analects
check.why: The Analects describe how to become a junzi.

check.q: What does Analects 15.24 teach?
choices: Do not impose on others what you do not wish for yourself
check.why: 15.24 gives the principle of reciprocity.

check.q: How do the grounds of duty differ between the Analects and the Gita?
choices: Confucius stresses learning, ritual and humaneness; the Gita grounds duty in teaching about the self and God
check.why: Both value roles but for different reasons.

lessons.title: Ahimsa in Jain and Buddhist Texts
lessons.mainIdea: Jain and Buddhist texts teach ahimsa, non-harming, with great seriousness, and Gandhi drew on these traditions too.
reading: *Ahimsa*, non-harming, is a key value in Jainism. The Acaranga Sutra, one of the oldest Jain texts, teaches that all breathing, living beings should not be killed, harmed or abused. Jain monks and nuns sweep their path to avoid harming insects. Gandhi grew up in Gujarat among Jain neighbors and counted a Jain teacher, Shrimad Rajchandra, as a guide.

The Dhammapada also teaches non-harming. Verses 129 and 130 say that all tremble at violence and all fear death; putting oneself in another's place, one should not kill or cause to kill. Verse 5 says that hatred is never ended by hatred, but by non-hatred; this is an eternal law.

The Gita lists ahimsa among good qualities (for example 16.2), yet it is set in a war. Hindus have held many views on how these fit together. Gandhi read the Gita through ahimsa. Others read it as allowing just war. Comparing texts helps readers see where each tradition places non-harming among its values.

words.d: non-harming; central in Jainism and valued in Hindu and Buddhist texts
one of the oldest Jain scriptures, teaching non-harming of all living beings
an Indian religion teaching strict non-harming, taught by Mahavira and earlier Tirthankaras

look.title: Dhammapada 5
look.text: Hatred is never ended by hatred in this world; it is ended by non-hatred. This is an eternal law.
look.cite: Dhammapada 5, paraphrased from F. Max Müller, The Dhammapada (Sacred Books of the East 10, 1881)
look.prompt: How might a nonviolent movement use this verse? Compare it with Gita 2.62–2.63 on anger.

check.q: Which religion treats ahimsa as a central value, with monks sweeping their path?
check.why: Jain monastics take great care not to harm living beings.

check.q: What does Dhammapada 5 say ends hatred?
check.why: Hatred ends by non-hatred.

check.q: Which Jain teacher did Gandhi count as a guide?
check.why: Gandhi named Rajchandra as an important influence.

lessons.title: The Sermon on the Mount
lessons.mainIdea: The Sermon on the Mount teaches loving enemies and not returning evil for evil, and it shaped Tolstoy, Gandhi and King.
reading: In Matthew 5 to 7, Jesus teaches a crowd on a mountain. He blesses the peacemakers (5:9). He says not to resist an evildoer with force but to turn the other cheek (5:39). He says to love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you (5:44). Christians have read these words in many ways, from strict pacifism to guidance for personal life.

Tolstoy read the Sermon as a strict command of nonviolence. Gandhi said the Sermon went straight to his heart when he first read it in London, and that he saw it as close to the Gita's teaching. He combined them in his own method, satyagraha. Christians and Hindus have since discussed whether his blend was faithful to each text.

Readers point to likenesses: both texts teach acting without seeking reward (Matthew 6:1 to 6:4; Gita 2.47). They also note differences: the Sermon speaks of a loving Father in heaven; the Gita speaks of Krishna and the eternal self, and it is set on a battlefield. Christians and Hindus each read their own scripture in their own tradition's terms.

words.d: the belief that war and violence are always wrong
Gandhi's nonviolent resistance, holding to truth
one who works to make peace; blessed in Matthew 5:9

look.title: Without Seeking Reward
look.text: Matthew 6:3–4 (paraphrase): when you give to the poor, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing, so that your giving is in secret. Gita 2.47 (paraphrase): your concern is with the action, never with its fruits.
look.prompt: What does each passage say about reward? Who or what, in each text, stands behind the action?

check.q: Which verse says to love your enemies?
check.why: Matthew 5:44 teaches love of enemies.

check.q: How did Gandhi describe his first reading of the Sermon on the Mount?
choices: It went straight to his heart
check.why: Gandhi wrote that it went straight to his heart.

check.q: Which idea do both Matthew 6 and Gita 2.47 share?
check.why: Both teach action free from seeking reward.

lessons.title: Bhakti and the Psalms
lessons.mainIdea: The Gita's bhakti and the Psalms both speak of trust and longing for God, in different words and settings.
reading: The Psalms are 150 songs and prayers in the Hebrew Bible, sung in Jewish and Christian worship for centuries. Psalm 23 pictures God as a shepherd who leads, restores and protects. Psalm 42 opens with longing: as a deer longs for streams of water, so my soul longs for you, O God.

The Gita's chapters on *bhakti* also speak of trust and closeness. Krishna says he accepts a leaf or flower offered with love (9.26) and that his devotee does not perish (9.31). Later bhakti poets, such as Mirabai and the Tamil Alvars, speak of longing for God in words close in feeling to the Psalms.

Differences matter. The Psalms address the God of Israel, known through covenant and history; they include laments, cries for justice and songs of the whole people. Hindu bhakti is addressed to Krishna, Rama, Shiva or the Goddess, often through a murti in a temple or home. Comparing them shows that devotion is a shared human form with many distinct voices.

words.d: 150 songs and prayers in the Hebrew Bible
a song or prayer of grief or complaint
in the Hebrew Bible, the binding relationship between God and Israel

look.title: Two Songs of Trust
look.text: Psalm 23 (paraphrase): the Lord is my shepherd; I lack nothing; though I walk through the darkest valley, I will fear no evil. Gita 9.31 (paraphrase): know for certain that my devotee does not perish.
look.prompt: What image does each text use for the divine's care? How does the speaker differ in each (who is speaking to whom)?

check.q: How many psalms are in the Book of Psalms?
check.why: The Book of Psalms has 150 psalms.

check.q: What image does Psalm 23 use for God?
check.why: Psalm 23 opens with the shepherd image.

check.q: Which is a real difference between the Psalms and Hindu bhakti?
choices: The Psalms address the God of Israel through covenant; bhakti addresses Krishna, Shiva, the Goddess and others
check.why: Each tradition's devotion has its own object and setting.

lessons.title: Bhakti and Sufi Poetry
lessons.mainIdea: Sufi poets and Hindu bhakti poets both sang of longing for the divine, and in India they sometimes shared audiences and images.
reading: Sufism is a tradition within Islam that stresses inward love of God. The Persian poet Rumi (1207 to 1273) opens his Masnavi with a reed flute that cries because it was cut from its reed bed; it longs to return to its source. Many readers see this as a picture of the soul longing for God.

Hindu bhakti poets also sing of separation and longing, called viraha. Krishna's flute is itself a famous image: in the Bhagavata Purana, the cowherd women of Vraj leave everything when they hear it. In India, bhakti and Sufi poets lived side by side for centuries. Kabir (15th century) drew from both and was claimed by Hindus and Muslims alike.

A careful comparison notices that both use the flute and longing, but they mean different things. For Rumi, the reed longs for God as understood in Islam, the One with no partner. For Krishna devotees, the flute is Krishna's call to the soul. Comparing them shows how shared images carry different meanings in different traditions.

words.d: a tradition within Islam stressing inward love and knowledge of God
the pain of separation from the beloved, a key feeling in bhakti poetry
a 15th-century poet-saint of North India honored by Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs

look.title: Two Flutes
look.text: Rumi, Masnavi 1 (paraphrase): listen to the reed; it cries of separation since it was cut from the reed bed. Bhagavata Purana, book 10 (paraphrase): when Krishna plays his flute in the forest, the cowherd women leave their work and run toward the sound.
look.prompt: In one image the flute cries; in the other it calls. What does that difference suggest about each tradition's picture of longing?

check.q: What image opens Rumi's Masnavi?
choices: A lamp in a windless place
A reed flute crying for its source
check.why: The Masnavi begins with the song of the reed.

check.q: What is viraha?
choices: The pain of separation from the beloved
check.why: Viraha is longing in separation.

check.q: Who was Kabir?
choices: A 15th-century poet-saint honored by Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs
check.why: Kabir drew on bhakti and Sufi traditions.

review.q: What is the main goal of comparison in this chapter?
choices: To understand each text better without ranking
To show all scriptures are identical
To replace one scripture with another
review.why: Comparison without ranking is the academic approach.

review.q: Which text contains God's answer from the whirlwind?
What view of the self distinguishes Buddhist teaching from the Gita?
review.why: Buddhists teach anatman; the Gita teaches atman.

review.q: What is ren in the Analects?
Which tradition's monks sweep their path to avoid harming insects?

review.why: Tolstoy's letter argued for nonviolent resistance.

review.q: Which Psalm pictures God as a shepherd?
Whose poem opens with the song of the reed flute?
